content: 1. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) does not recommend the addition of any biological tests to current methods for diagnosing leprosy under programmatic conditions. This is due to the insufficient diagnostic accuracy of most tests studied, their lack of commercial or clinical availability, and their infeasibility for use in field settings. Current evidence does not demonstrate a clear advantage of these tests over clinical diagnosis or confirmatory tests like slit-skin smears or skin biopsies. 2. The interpretation of positive test results among household contacts is challenging, as it is difficult to distinguish between false positives and indications of preclinical infection. Additionally, the costs of such tests have not been reviewed. 3. There are no subgroup considerations or new implementation concerns, as the current approach relies on existing practices. Similarly, there are no new monitoring or evaluation concerns. 4. Research priorities include testing promising assays with greater diagnostic accuracy in larger, well-designed studies to assess their effectiveness in detecting infection among contacts. 5. There is no diagnostic test for detecting M. leprae infection (latent leprosy) among contacts that has sufficient sensitivity and specificity and is feasible under programmatic conditions. The GDG strongly recommends against using tests to identify contacts at higher risk of developing leprosy due to the low accuracy of the tests studied and the lack of cost review. 6. Under the Global Leprosy Strategy, contacts of leprosy patients (household or social contacts) are screened for leprosy shortly after the detection and treatment of the index case and then annually for five years. Preventive treatment with single-dose rifampicin (SDR) has shown some efficacy, but the availability of a test for infection could help target more specific and effective preventive interventions. 7. A systematic review of seven studies with at least one year of follow-up on the predictive utility of ELISA for anti-PGL-1 in contacts showed low sensitivity (median 26%), high specificity (median 89%), and low positive predictive value (median 4%). The quality of evidence was graded as low due to moderate risk of bias and serious inconsistency. 8. The GDG concluded that the treatment of all contacts with an effective, inexpensive, and safe preventive tool might be an effective public health intervention. However, the availability of a test for infection would help target preventive actions more effectively and facilitate early detection among those with latent infection. 9. Regarding a single treatment regimen for all leprosy patients, the GDG considered the possibility of using a uniform multidrug therapy (UMDT) regimen with three drugs for six months. This could simplify treatment, reduce misclassification of patients, and improve outcomes for paucibacillary (PB) leprosy patients. However, evidence for its effectiveness in multibacillary (MB) leprosy patients is limited, with some data suggesting a non-statistically significant trend toward increased relapse risk compared to the standard 12-month regimen. 10. For PB leprosy, evidence suggests that a three-drug six-month regimen may improve clinical and histological outcomes compared to the current two-drug six-month regimen. For MB leprosy, there is insufficient evidence to shorten the duration of the three-drug therapy from 12 to six months. 11. The GDG emphasized the importance of effective treatments for leprosy due to its significant clinical, social, and public health consequences. A single regimen effective for all types of leprosy would be desirable, especially in primary healthcare settings where expertise in leprosy classification may be limited. 12. The overall certainty of evidence for the effects of UMDT versus MB-MDT in MB leprosy patients is low, based on one randomized controlled trial (RCT) and other quasi-randomized or non-randomized studies. For PB leprosy, there is some evidence of better clinical outcomes with a three-drug regimen, but data on side effects and compliance are limited. 13. The GDG concluded that using a three-drug PB regimen for six months might improve clinical outcomes, but there is insufficient evidence to recommend shortening the duration of three-drug therapy for MB patients.
